construction.credential: The account credential is a WebAuthn discoverable credential on the account services RP ID, created at account creation. It is asymmetric, so the service stores public material only -- which is what §16.1s inventory row already said it stored.
construction.alg_list: pubKeyCredParams is fixed and ordered and is part of the carrier version: -8 (Ed25519) then -7 (ES256). RS256 is declined. Both offered algorithms verify in WebCrypto, so the offline verifier needs no polyfill.
construction.no_stretching: None, for the third time and on the strongest of the three arguments. Rows 13 and 14 answered "Argon2id or none" with none because a generated 125-bit code leaves no entropy deficit for a work factor to cover. Here there is no secret in the profile at all: the private key is in the authenticator, so a profile holder holds a public key and a verification routine, and grinding it means forging a signature.
construction.extensions: None. This role uses no WebAuthn extension, which is why it can root on the authenticator where §13.3s device lock could not: PRF is an extension whose availability is a matrix of OS, browser and authenticator kind, and a signature is the core of the API.
construction.binding: One service-signed binding per credential, stored in the device-local slot index (§6.5). message = LP("done/slotbind/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(account_id) || LP(principal_id) || LP(rp_id) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(cred_id) || LP(hex public_key), signed with Ed25519 by the epochs authorization key.
construction.public_key_encoding: SubjectPublicKeyInfo, matched against a compiled-in set of two prefixes -- Ed25519 and P-256. The algorithm is inside the bound bytes rather than in a field beside them, so there is no separate alg to bind and nothing to renegotiate.
construction.anchor: The service signature is the constructions load-bearing part. An asymmetric verifier removes the guessable secret and introduces a substitutable public key, and a public key in a structured clone is exactly as editable as row 3s kind. Verified against the lineage the client already retains (§13.5), a substitution needs the services private key rather than write access to IndexedDB.
construction.challenge: challenge = SHA-256( LP("done/slotunlock/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(principal_id) || LP(cred_id) || LP(hex nonce) ), with 32 fresh random nonce bytes per attempt. Row 14 §5s rule: bind the assertion to the operation, not to a clock.
construction.verification_order: Binding signature, then bound credential id, then client data (parsed, never rebuilt), then authenticator data with UV required, then the assertion signature under the algorithm the stored encoding names. The binding is first because everything after it trusts a public key that came out of a structured clone.
construction.sign_count: Read and ignored. See the demonstrations.
construction.grants: Nothing on the network. No relay token, no account session, no authorization change (§13.9). The service never issued this challenge, so the assertion is not one it will accept.
construction.length_prefix: uint16be(byteLength) || utf8 -- injective, so no field can shift another.

authorization.role: The service's authorization key for this epoch (§13.5). Signs slot bindings; holds no content key.

passkey.role: The account credential, where the authenticator offers Ed25519 (COSE -8).

attacker.role: The attacker's own passkey. Whoever can edit the slot index can enroll one of these with their own authenticator; what they cannot do is get the service to sign for it.

es256_credential.role: The account credential where the authenticator offers ES256 (COSE -7).
es256_credential.source: Generated for this file; d and (x, y) are checked against each other on every run.

binding_vectors.name: laptop-ed25519
binding_vectors.why: The preferred case: an authenticator offering COSE -8, so the credential adds no primitive to row 1s suite.

inputs.public_key_note: SubjectPublicKeyInfo, as PublicKeyCredential.getPublicKey() returns. The algorithm (COSE -8) is inside these bytes and is not a separate bound field

binding_vectors.name: phone-es256
binding_vectors.why: The ordinary case, and the reason ES256 is in the suite at all: the authenticator chose it. Verified in WebCrypto with no polyfill.

inputs.public_key_note: SubjectPublicKeyInfo, as PublicKeyCredential.getPublicKey() returns. The algorithm (COSE -7) is inside these bytes and is not a separate bound field

assertion_vectors.name: laptop-ed25519
assertion_vectors.why: Fully pinned: Ed25519 is deterministic, so the signature is a fact about the construction.

assertion_vectors.name: phone-es256
assertion_vectors.why: Pinned except the signature. ECDSA's is randomized, so publishing one would pin this generator's RNG rather than the construction. The generator mints and verifies one on every run instead, and the file carries the bytes that are actually specified.

demonstrations.name: sign-count-is-read-and-ignored
demonstrations.why: An assertion reporting signCount 3 where the last one reported 0 verifies, deliberately. WebAuthn's counter exists to detect a cloned authenticator, and a synced passkey -- iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, any credential that follows the person rather than the device -- cannot maintain one and reports zero forever. A verifier enforcing monotonicity refuses the ordinary case while detecting nothing, so this row does not enforce it, and says so here rather than leaving the omission to look like an oversight.

demonstrations.name: binding-outlives-a-revocation-this-device-has-not-seen
demonstrations.why: A binding signed in epoch 7 still verifies on a device that has never seen epoch 8, so a credential revoked while this slot was closed still reopens it offline. That is a bound rather than a defect, and §13.9 is what bounds it: reopening grants no relay token, no account session and no authorization change, so what a stale binding opens is already-local state and nothing else. §13.5's lineage closes it the moment the device is online.
demonstrations.expected: opens, and grants nothing on the network

must_fail.name: forged-binding-under-other-key
must_fail.why: The whole attack, executed competently: substitute your own public key into the slot index, assert with your own authenticator, and re-sign the binding so the record is internally consistent. It fails on the one thing in the profile a profile holder cannot produce.

must_fail.name: unknown-key-algorithm
must_fail.why: A service-signed binding carrying an X25519 SubjectPublicKeyInfo -- valid DER, right length, key-agreement rather than verification. The accepted encodings are a compiled-in set of two, and anything outside it is refused rather than guessed at. Row 1s rule about carrier versions, at the one place this design has a key type to choose.

must_fail.name: unbound-credential
must_fail.why: An assertion from a credential the binding does not name -- an attacker enrolling their own passkey on this device.

must_fail.name: uv-flag-clear
must_fail.why: User presence without user verification. The gate is *verification*: a UP-only assertion is a click, and a click is what the person at a shared keyboard already has.

must_fail.name: wrong-rp-id-hash
must_fail.why: An assertion collected for another relying party, presented with an honest binding. This is what a phishing origin obtains, and it fails before any signature is checked.

must_fail.name: wrong-origin
must_fail.why: The same from the client-data side. The two are checked separately because they can disagree.

must_fail.name: wrong-client-data-type
must_fail.why: A registration ceremony presented as an assertion. webauthn.create and webauthn.get sign the same shape.

must_fail.name: framed-ceremony
must_fail.why: A complete, correctly signed assertion collected in a delegated iframe: this origin, this RP ID, this challenge, crossOrigin true. The origin check does not cover it -- in a cross-origin frame the caller IS the legitimate app origin while the top-level one differs -- and the policy is same-origin only (S0-1, P-5). CSP frame-ancestors none makes the frame unreachable and is row 17s; this is the half the repository can verify.

must_fail.name: embedding-origin-claimed
must_fail.why: Client data carrying crossOrigin false AND a topOrigin, signed over its own bytes. The specification emits topOrigin only when crossOrigin is true, so this is a client contradicting itself -- and a verifier reading only the boolean accepts an embedding recorded in the bytes it just hashed. Separate from the one above on purpose: a negative setting both would pass with either check present and prove neither.

must_fail.name: flipped-signature-bit
must_fail.why: The signature doing its own job.

must_fail.name: challenge-rewritten-to-match
must_fail.why: Row 9s lesson, and the reason the challenge negatives below are not enough alone. They fail on a string comparison, which fails whether or not the signature covers the challenge. This one rewrites clientDataJSON to carry the challenge the verifier wants, so the comparison passes and only the signature can refuse it -- which is also the real attack, since clientDataJSON arrives from the same place the assertion does.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-label
must_fail.why: The domain-separation label, isolated. It is the whole of what stops a service signature of another kind being read as a slot binding.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-version
must_fail.why: Row 1s rule: a carrier version selects the suite, so a renumbered binding must fail rather than select a weaker one.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-account-id
must_fail.why: Another account's binding on the same device. PRD §6.7s two-principal profile is the ordinary case, not an attack.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-principal-id
must_fail.why: A binding lifted between slots on one profile, which is the substitution that needs no forgery if the slot is not named.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-rp-id
must_fail.why: A consistent assertion for another relying party, presented with a binding edited to name it. The obvious negative fails on the rpIdHash comparison whether or not the binding covers rp_id; this one satisfies that comparison, so only the binding can refuse it.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-epoch
must_fail.why: Which authorization epoch admitted this credential (§13.5). It is what bounds a binding naming a since-revoked credential.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-cred-id
must_fail.why: The credential id, isolated from the key beside it: an implementation binding the key and not the id accepts a rebound identifier.

must_fail.name: aad-only-binding-public-key
must_fail.why: The field this row exists to bind, and the negative that shows what its absence costs: the attackers key in the record *and* the attackers assertion, with the honest service signature left in place. Without public_key in the signed message this opens, because the attacker supplies a consistent pair. IndexedDB holds a structured clone, so that pair is one property edit away.

must_fail.name: aad-only-challenge-label
must_fail.why: The cross-protocol negative. The same credential authenticates to the service, so an assertion is a proof two different verifiers read. The label is the purpose, and without it a slot-unlock assertion has the shape of a sign-in.

must_fail.name: aad-only-challenge-version
must_fail.why: The challenge carrier version, isolated from the binding version, because they are separate carriers and an implementation can bind one and not the other.

must_fail.name: aad-only-challenge-principal-id
must_fail.why: An assertion minted to open one slot, presented at another on the same profile.

must_fail.name: aad-only-challenge-cred-id
must_fail.why: An assertion minted naming one credential, presented as another. The account has several and they are equally able to assert.

must_fail.name: aad-only-challenge-nonce
must_fail.why: Replay. Without the nonce the challenge is a constant per slot, and one captured assertion opens it forever.

primitive_kats: Ed25519, SHA-256 and HKDF KATs are row 1's, in test/vectors/algorithm-suite.json. This generator checks that row 1 still selects Ed25519 for signatures and still publishes its known-answer test, so the two documents fail apart rather than drift apart.
